analysis.one_liner: Bans the IRS from offering its own free tax filing option, killing Direct File.
analysis.headline: The bill to shut down the IRS's free Direct File program was introduced January 15, 2025 with a Republican sponsor and 29 Republican cosponsors, and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee without a markup or vote ever since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes into law that the Treasury Secretary may not prepare tax returns, and specifically outlaws Direct File — the free IRS-run system that lets taxpayers in 25 participating states prepare and file their federal returns online at no cost. It preserves the Free File program, in which taxpayers file free returns through third-party commercial software, and the VITA program, which funds community groups to help low-income and disabled filers. It also bars the Treasury Department from spending money on grants or contracts to build or run any government electronic tax preparation service. If enacted, taxpayers who today file free and directly with the IRS would instead have to go through commercial software or volunteer assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial tax-preparation software companies are the main beneficiary: Direct File is a free public competitor to their paid products, and this bill would shut it down and block the IRS from building a successor. Taxpayers who prefer private software lose nothing, since Free File and commercial products remain available.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the IRS from preparing federal returns or refund claims and specifically treats any return filed through an IRS-run electronic tax preparation service — Direct File — as prohibited [S2][S3].
It bars Treasury from awarding grants or entering contracts for the development or operation of an electronic tax preparation service, foreclosing a government-run successor program [S2][S3].

It preserves the Free File program (free filing through third-party commercial software) and the VITA grant program for low-income and disabled filers, so free options routed through private software remain [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers in the 25 states where Direct File operates would lose the only filing channel that is both free and run by the government itself; they would pay preparer fees or navigate commercial free-file products with income limits and upsells. The public also loses a taxpayer-funded system it already paid to build.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers who use free IRS Direct File

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates the only free filing option that does not route taxpayers through a commercial company; Direct File currently serves qualified taxpayers in 25 states at no cost [S2].
The prohibition on Treasury grants and contracts goes beyond Direct File itself, blocking any future government-developed electronic filing service even if Congress later wanted one [S3].

Supporters argue the government is duplicating software that private companies already offer for free through Free File, so the bill saves public money; the counter is that Free File's free tier comes with eligibility limits and commercial upselling that Direct File does not have [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to one industry: removing a free public competitor protects the market for paid tax software and preparers. The costs fall on ordinary taxpayers who would lose a free, straightforward way to file and on the treasury, which already invested in the program. Free File remains, but it is administered through the same commercial companies the bill protects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Adrian Smith (R-NE) introduced the FAIR PREP Act on January 15, 2025 with 10 original cosponsors, all Republicans [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the full action history shows no markup, hearing, vote, or further action since [S1][S5].
The bill eventually drew 29 cosponsors, all of them Republicans [S4].
The IRS Direct File program the bill targets is a free filing portal available to qualified taxpayers in 25 participating states [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, taxpayers who use Direct File are better off, because the bill has not advanced and the free IRS filing program remains in place. The tax-preparation industry gains only if the bill later moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers using free IRS Direct File, for now

for.name: Adrian Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit IRS return preparation and Direct File, and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 29 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Democrat did.

for.name: Tax-preparation software industry
for.role: Commercial tax software and preparers (e.g., Intuit, H&R Block)
for.what_they_did: Long-standing opponents of government-run free filing, the industry's products stand to gain market protection from the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over the tax code
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the January 2025 referral — no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Republican — the sponsor plus 29 of 223 Republicans — and no Democrat has signed on.

industries.note: Direct File is a free government-run competitor to paid tax software; the bill shuts it down and bans Treasury from building a successor, protecting the companies' market. Their gain is paid preparer fees for taxpayers who now file free.

industries.industry: Free File program partners (commercial software firms)
industries.note: The bill expressly preserves Free File, which routes free federal filing through third-party commercial software. That keeps private companies the gatekeepers of free filing, with eligibility limits and upselling, rather than a direct government channel.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in Ways and Means for months without a markup rarely get floor votes on their own. The likelier path for this proposal is riding along in a larger tax package; until then, Direct File continues to operate and the bill's chances of a standalone vote are low.
